implementation_notes: A Ruby Hash is the document, and Ruby's own classes cover the view half: Struct gives a fixed member set with readers plus [] / to_h, its immutable successor Data is stricter and frozen, OpenStruct is documented as a hash-backed object that defines attributes through method_missing and define_singleton_method, and dry-struct adds coercing, validated typed attributes over the same hash. The trait interfaces collapse into modules (mixins) or plain reader methods. Because Hash keys may be any object, use symbol keys inside the program and convert at the JSON boundary; keep OpenStruct for scripts and tests, since it defines singleton methods per instance.
code_sketch:
doc = { model: "300SL", price: 100 }        # loosely typed document
Car = Struct.new(:model, :price)           # typed view over known keys
car = Car.new(*doc.values_at(:model, :price))
car.model                                   # => "300SL"
dynamic = OpenStruct.new(doc)               # arbitrary attributes at runtime
dynamic.price                               # => 100
pitfalls: OpenStruct defines a singleton method per attribute and can clobber methods inherited from Object; its documentation warns it is unsuitable for performance-sensitive code, and a misspelled attribute returns nil instead of raising.
JSON.parse without symbolize_names produces string keys, so doc[:model] silently returns nil where doc["model"] works - normalise keys at the boundary.
Hash is mutable and shared by reference: two views over one hash can rewrite each other's data; use freeze or Data for documents that must not change.
